Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

   one a night, each looking like a fresh incident.

   **Pass `--pr` on any park a pull request or an issue would end**, not only on an
   approval, where it is required. It stamps `Ends-when: #<n> closed` on the item, and
   that is what makes the park end by itself: the janitor closes the item `done` when
   the target merges and `rejected` when it is closed unmerged. Without it the park
   stands until a person happens to read it.

   **A marked issue needs no write-back at all**: it is the item, so the approval
   park it wears *is* the in-review state and the failure park *is* the report (which
   is why `--pr` is still required on an approval — a park nobody can act on is not
   a park). The standing status is also what stops the next scheduler run adopting
   the same issue again; clearing it is a person's decision, made after reading what
   the run said. Only an item filed under the older shadow model writes back to a
   different issue, and the command does that too.

   Only `task:status:needs-human-failure` (and a park whose kind cannot be decoded) holds the
   task's lane — while one is open the generator files no further occurrence of
   this task. The other three wait for their human while the schedule carries on,
   so leaving one open costs nobody but the person it names.

   The `claudinite-task-exec` record goes onto the item, in the same comment, and
   the command writes it — Actions logs expire and the item does not, so the item
   is where a record has to live. Nothing here is yours to print by hand.

7. **Capture this session before you end it.** Last step, after the item is
   converged, and run it whichever way step 6 went:

   ```bash
   CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE=<n> node <engine>/hooks/session-end-command.mjs
   ```

   That runner invokes whatever session-end steps this repo's declared packs
   contribute; it knows nothing about what any of them do, and a repo that
   contributes none does nothing. Nobody is sitting in front of this session, so it
   ends by having its container reclaimed — precisely the ending that fires no
   `SessionEnd` hook. Left to the hook, every unattended run would leave no record
   of itself anywhere: not of the skills it loaded, not of the checks that caught
   something, not of how the work actually went, and not of the record you just
   printed. `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE` is what files those logs under the item that
   ran, rather than under nothing.

   It cannot fail your run — the item is already converged and this changes nothing
   on GitHub. If it reports an error, **say so plainly in your final message** and
   end anyway.

## The one standing bound

You execute **this one item and nothing else**. Never list other work items,
never sweep the queue, never act on a second issue in this session — however
obviously stuck another one looks. Recovery is code that runs elsewhere, and a
session that helps out is how one item becomes three duplicate PRs.

Tool selection guidance:

## The landscape

| Vendor | Self-serve | Entry cost | Per participant | Turnaround | Panel |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Lyssna](https://www.lyssna.com/pricing/) | Yes | **Free** (3 seats, 15 self-recruited responses); Growth $166/mo | ~$1/credit, **1 credit per test-minute per response**; +2 credits with a screener | hours | consumer, own panel |

| [Prolific](https://www.prolific.com/pricing) | Yes | none, PAYG wallet | your reward + **42.8%** platform fee (33.3% academic); floor £6.00/hr, recommended £9.00/hr | hours | research panel, UK-origin |
| [UserTesting](https://www.usertesting.com/pricing) | Free single test | **not published** — Advanced / Ultimate / Ultimate+, "Request pricing" | n/a | **"typically in less than an hour"** for the free test | consumer |
| [Maze](https://maze.co/pricing/) | — | **no prices published at all**; the pricing page is a feature table plus "Contact sales" | n/a | — | consumer |
| [Wynter](https://wynter.com/pricing) | Yes (also PAYG) | **$20,000/yr** Pro · $40,000 Elite · $100,000 Black | n/a | **"<48hr"**, stated | **B2B only**, 86K verified |

**What's distinct about each.** Lyssna is the cheap quantitative fork-in-the-road tool — five-second tests, preference tests, first-click tests against static images. UserInterviews is recruitment-first (now with screeners, scheduling and recording/transcription in beta) — the way to get five screened humans on a call. Prolific is the cheapest per head with the best screening, but you supply the stimulus. UserTesting is the think-aloud **video** incumbent: you watch the confusion rather than infer it. Maze does prototype analytics (heatmaps, misclick, time-on-task) but won't tell you what it costs without a sales conversation. Wynter is B2B positioning feedback and is priced out of reach for anything at this scale.

## Recommendation for a single experiment under £300

1. **UserTesting's free single test** — one think-aloud video of a real person using the live site, in under an hour, for £0. Highest information-per-pound available anywhere on this list.
2. **Lyssna's free plan plus panel credits** — a 5-minute preference test across ~40 UK participants is roughly $200 in credits with no subscription. Two rival redesigns, judged by strangers, in an afternoon.
3. **UserInterviews** ($49/session + incentive) when the idea is novel enough that you need to hear *why*, not just *which*.

Skip Maze until it publishes prices; skip Wynter entirely.

## Why this fits our pipeline unusually well

The executable-requirements harness already renders every UI state as a committed, deterministic golden under `product/requirements.md`. Those PNGs are **directly usable as Lyssna or Maze stimuli with no extra work** — which inverts the normal order. Instead of build → ship → hope, we can do: write the leaf → refresh the golden → put the picture in front of 40 strangers → build only what survives. The goldens are already the owner's approval surface; this makes them a *market's* approval surface too.

That is the interesting part, and it is the part that generalises past this repo.

## Future work: a claudinite pack for this

The loop above is mechanical enough to be a pack, and nothing about it is Fringe-specific — it applies to any repo running `spec-driven-product` + `executable-requirements`. Sketch of what it would own:

- **A rule about where a design decision gets settled.** Today a brave UI idea is settled by the owner's judgment in a chat message. The pack's rule would be: a change that alters what the product's users *see or decide with* is a candidate for external validation before implementation, and name the threshold at which that's worth $200.
- **A skill — `validate-with-users`** — carrying the procedure: pick the leaf, export its golden (and its rival), write the task and screener, place the order, read the result back. The vendor mechanics are exactly what a `SKILL.md` is for, and exactly what nobody remembers between experiments.
- **The result as a committed artifact.** A verdict that lives in a vendor dashboard is lost. The pack would land it beside the leaf it judged — so `product/requirements.md` eventually says not just "the owner approved this picture" but "*n* people preferred it, on this date". That is the piece with real compounding value, and no vendor gives it to you.
- **A `verify-in-production`-shaped follow-up.** A validated design that ships should come back later against the behaviour it predicted.

Open questions before anyone builds it: whether the vendor APIs support placing an order programmatically (unchecked); whether one pack should own both the *deciding* and the *running*, or whether the decision rule belongs in `spec-driven-product`; and whether the sample sizes affordable at this budget are large enough that recording a verdict in the spec is honest rather than false precision.

## The idea

Publish a manifest listing every downloadable data file and a hash of its contents. Fetch it on each load, and evict exactly the cached entries whose hash has moved.

## Why it's better than what we have

The current TTLs (`shared/data-cache.js`) are guesses about how fast each file changes — four days for the catalogue, one for availability, seven for descriptions. They price the same bet on every file and get it wrong in both directions at once: too long and visitors read stale data, too short and they re-download something that never changed.

A manifest gives **longer caching and fresher data at the same time**, which no TTL can. It also makes #309 structurally impossible: every file is checked against one manifest from one publish, so a visitor can't hold Thursday's catalogue beside Saturday's sidecar.

## Design notes

- **The manifest is the one file that must never carry a TTL.** Nothing can attest to its own freshness — a stale copy carries a valid hash of itself. Caching the manifest doesn't save a round-trip, it moves the staleness up one level and hides it better.
- **Marginal cost is near zero.** The planner already fetches `package.json` uncached on every load for the version pill (visible in the reporter's network trace). The manifest is the same shape of request and could absorb that one.
- **Record the hash, don't re-hash.** Store the manifest hash in the stamps map beside the entry; the freshness check is then a string compare. Re-hashing means pushing megabytes through a digest on the critical path to answer a question the bookkeeping already knows.
- **Written atomically with the assets** — same `write_derived_outputs()` call in `scraper/normalize.py`, so it can't describe a publish that didn't happen.
- **A deploy race is expected**: manifest fetched, deploy lands, asset fetched, hash disagrees. Refetch once and continue; only a mismatch surviving fresh copies of both is a real fault.
- Size is not a substitute for a hash: applying #274's correction to the Aug 7 catalogue changes 0 bytes of 3,140,534 while changing the meaning of every record.

## Relationship to the #309 fix

# Single-issue triage

Triage **one** open issue and take the **first** applicable action. This **acts** — but every action
defaults to the reversible option when the check is inconclusive.

- **Already implemented in `main`** → **close** (`completed`) + a one-line comment citing where it
  landed.
- **Conflicts with a current guideline** → label `needs-decision` + a comment naming the conflict.
- **Blocked by another issue** → label `blocked` + a comment `blocked by #N`.
- **Small and quick to do** → label `quick-win` + a comment scoping it.
- **Else** → leave it.

**Every checkbox in the issue body ticked** is the author's own claim that the work is done — the
strongest completion signal an issue can carry, and the one thing that puts an otherwise quiet issue
into the first rung. It is **a claim, not proof**: read it as a reason to run the implemented-in-`main`
check, never as the answer. Verified ⇒ close; not ⇒ comment naming what is still missing. A
partially-ticked list is not a completion signal at all — triage the issue as if it carried no boxes.
Where the ask has **no repo-side artifact** (a console setting, a routine only a human can touch), those
ticks by the issue's own author are the closing condition — say so and close.

**"Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s content _now_** — confirm
it there and cite it. **Never** infer it from a linked PR merging or the issue merely looking done. If
you can't point to it, **comment, don't close.** Create a label if it's missing. Return `{ action,
note }` (action one of closed/needs-decision/blocked/quick-win/left/unchanged).

## Never re-post a verdict you already posted

A triage comment updates the issue, and an updated issue is the next window's touched-issue
trigger — so a comment that only restates the last one wakes this task again tomorrow, and again
the day after. The verdict is the news; re-deriving it is not.

Before writing anything, read the issue's comments and find the most recent one this task posted
— by its marker, or, on an issue triaged before the marker existed, by its wording. If the action
you are about to take is the one that comment already announced, **post nothing and change nothing**
(a label already on the issue included) and return `{ action: 'unchanged', note: '<action> since
<its date>' }`. Closing is never a repeat: it changes the issue's state and ends the sequence.

End every comment you post with this marker, alone on the last line:

```
<!-- claudinite:tidy-issues verdict=<action> -->
```

Website to help find a fringe show — **Fringe Discover**.

🌐 **Live site:** https://missingbulb.github.io/EdFringeNow/

A single-page site for finding the nearest Edinburgh Fringe show happening
right now ("Fringe Rush"): editable constraint cards (genre, travel mode, next
constraint), an interactive map of venues, and a gamified "discovery journey".

## The executable spec

What the UI must render and how it must behave is specified leaf by leaf in
[product/requirements.md](product/requirements.md) — a numbered spec where
every requirement is proven by exactly one executable case (a pixel-exact
golden, a driven-gesture assertion, or a pure-rule test). The framework, its
lanes and the owner-approval contract live in
[product/requirements/README.md](product/requirements/README.md).

## Running

No build step. Because the app fetches `data/shows.json`, serve the folder over
HTTP rather than opening the file directly:

```
python3 -m http.server 8000
# then open http://localhost:8000
```

## Tech

- Plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript (no framework, no build tools)
- [Leaflet](https://leafletjs.com/) + OpenStreetMap tiles for the map (no API key)
- Mock show data in `data/shows.json`

## Structure

```
index.html        page markup
css/styles.css    styling
js/app.js         data loading, map, show list, journey, editable cards
js/places.js      non-show places: Nominatim geocoding + partner booking links
data/shows.json   mock Edinburgh Fringe shows
```

## Tests & CI

The planner's computation engine (`plan/lib/`) is unit-tested with the built-in
Node test runner — no dependencies, no install:

```
npm test          # node --test plan/lib/__tests__/*.test.mjs
npm run verify     # tests + JS parse-checks (node --check) + Python py_compile
```

## Evidence

Four runs, three different outcomes, across trees whose only differences are under `.claudinite/` (a local-pack consolidation, #612 / #613 — no UI code, and `test:ui` itself untouched):

| Run | Tree | Result |
|---|---|---|
| CI, `ui-requirements` | #613 head `a083751` | fails `shared-money.8.5` — 3346 of 117840 px (2.84%) |
| local `npm run test:ui` | same commit `a083751` | fails `now-commitment.3.6` (1183 of 28512 px, 4.15%) **and** `now-filters.5.6` (animated golden, 81979 bytes committed vs 74845 rendered) |
| local `npm run test:ui` | same commit `a083751`, immediately after | **101/101 pass** |
| local `npm run test:ui` | `origin/main` `b4a2730` | 101/101 pass |

Four distinct cases have now flapped (`shared-money.8.5`, `now-commitment.3.6`, `now-filters.5.6`), which points at the harness rather than at any one case's capture.

The pack's own rule says the harness stays at zero pixel tolerance and that *"when the comparison ever flaps, the fix is more determinism, not a tolerance"* — so the remedy is to find what is still unpinned, not to widen the comparator. The determinism levers are all in `product/requirements/shared/harness/`: fixed clock via `page.clock`, fixed geolocation, seeded `Math.random`, route-fulfilled network, frozen animations, the `FONTCONFIG_FILE` font subset, and the pinned Chromium. Something outside that set is still leaking in.

Worth checking first, given the local runs above were on a machine with the fonts subset in play and still flapped: an async settle that `case-helpers.js` does not wait on (the pages settle their async work into observable state — a capture racing that would explain a small, varying pixel delta), and whether `--test-concurrency=1` is actually holding for the behavior lane as well as the screen lane.

#613 is a local-pack consolidation. Making the harness deterministic is a real fix but a different change, and doing it there would widen that PR well past its request.

{"number":610,"title":"UX research services: what's available, what they cost, and a case for a claudinite pack","body":"Reference notes from a 2026-09-04 survey, prompted by the question: is there a service that gives a **real-human assessment of a UI/UX idea within 24–72 hours**, so we can experiment more bravely than "build it and hope"?

Yes — the category is unmoderated remote user testing plus on-demand panel recruitment, and the turnaround we wanted is the product these sell. Every figure below was read from the vendor's own page on **2026-09-04**; prices move, so re-read before committing.

## The landscape

| Vendor | Self-serve | Entry cost | Per participant | Turnaround | Panel |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Lyssna](https://www.lyssna.com/pricing/) | Yes | **Free** (3 seats, 15 self-recruited responses); Growth $166/mo | ~$1/credit, **1 credit per test-minute per response**; +2 credits with a screener | hours | consumer, own panel |
| [UserInterviews](https://www.userinterviews.com/pricing) | Yes | none | **$49/session** PAYG ($98 advanced B2B; $41/$36 on annual) **plus** your incentive | ~48h | 7.5M panel |
| [Prolific](https://www.prolific.com/pricing) | Yes | none, PAYG wallet | your reward + **42.8%** platform fee (33.3% academic); floor £6.00/hr, recommended £9.00/hr | hours | research panel, UK-origin |
| [UserTesting](https://www.usertesting.com/pricing) | Free single test | **not published** — Advanced / Ultimate / Ultimate+, "Request pricing" | n/a | **"typically in less than an hour"** for the free test | consumer |
| [Maze](https://maze.co/pricing/) | — | **no prices published at all**; the pricing page is a feature table plus "Contact sales" | n/a | — | consumer |
| [Wynter](https://wynter.com/pricing) | Yes (also PAYG) | **$20,000/yr** Pro · $40,000 Elite · $100,000 Black | n/a | **"<48hr"**, stated | **B2B only**, 86K verified |

**What's distinct about each.** Lyssna is the cheap quantitative fork-in-the-road tool — five-second tests, preference tests, first-click tests against static images. UserInterviews is recruitment-first (now with screeners, scheduling and recording/transcription in beta) — the way to get five screened humans on a call. Prolific is the cheapest per head with the best screening, but you supply the stimulus. UserTesting is the think-aloud **video** incumbent: you watch the confusion rather than infer it. Maze does prototype analytics (heatmaps, misclick, time-on-task) but won't tell you what it costs without a sales conversation. Wynter is B2B positioning feedback and is priced out of reach for anything at this scale.

## Recommendation for a single experiment under £300

1. **UserTesting's free single test** — one think-aloud video of a real person using the live site, in under an hour, for £0. Highest information-per-pound available anywhere on this list.
2. **Lyssna's free plan plus panel credits** — a 5-minute preference test across ~40 UK participants is roughly $200 in credits with no subscription. Two rival redesigns, judged by strangers, in an afternoon.
3. **UserInterviews** ($49/session + incentive) when the idea is novel enough that you need to hear *why*, not just *which*.

Skip Maze until it publishes prices; skip Wynter entirely.

## Why this fits our pipeline unusually well

The executable-requirements harness already renders every UI state as a committed, deterministic golden under `product/requirements.md`. Those PNGs are **directly usable as Lyssna or Maze stimuli with no extra work** — which inverts the normal order. Instead of build → ship → hope, we can do: write the leaf → refresh the golden → put the picture in front of 40 strangers → build only what survives. The goldens are already the owner's approval surface; this makes them a *market's* approval surface too.

That is the interesting part, and it is the part that generalises past this repo.

## Future work: a claudinite pack for this

The loop above is mechanical enough to be a pack, and nothing about it is Fringe-specific — it applies to any repo running `spec-driven-product` + `executable-requirements`. Sketch of what it would own:

- **A rule about where a design decision gets settled.** Today a brave UI idea is settled by the owner's judgment in a chat message. The pack's rule would be: a change that alters what the product's users *see or decide with* is a candidate for external validation before implementation, and name the threshold at which that's worth $200.
- **A skill — `validate-with-users`** — carrying the procedure: pick the leaf, export its golden (and its rival), write the task and screener, place the order, read the result back. The vendor mechanics are exactly what a `SKILL.md` is for, and exactly what nobody remembers between experiments.
- **The result as a committed artifact.** A verdict that lives in a vendor dashboard is lost. The pack would land it beside the leaf it judged — so `product/requirements.md` eventually says not just "the owner approved this picture" but "*n* people preferred it, on this date". That is the piece with real compounding value, and no vendor gives it to you.
- **A `verify-in-production`-shaped follow-up.** A validated design that ships should come back later against the behaviour it predicted.

Open questions before anyone builds it: whether the vendor APIs support placing an order programmatically (unchecked); whether one pack should own both the *deciding* and the *running*, or whether the decision rule belongs in `spec-driven-product`; and whether the sample sizes affordable at this budget are large enough that recording a verdict in the spec is honest rather than false precision.

The pack belongs in the Claudinite canon rather than this repo's local packs — the territory is "shipping against an executable spec", not "the Fringe site" — so this issue is a note toward it, not a plan for here.

#165 added the planner's schedule-board nags ("Need a place to sleep?" in the night zone, "Transportation sorted?" on the first/last-day trip blocks), whose IDs live in `shared/affiliates.js` — not `js/places.js`. Sign-up steps and the programme comparison for those are in #164. What that means for this issue:

- **Step 1 (Booking.com) is shared work, done once.** One account issues one set of credentials; both pages spend them. Whoever completes step 1 should fill the planner's fields too, or this issue's "Done when" leaves the night nag untagged while the Now page's hotel pills earn.
- **The route needs deciding once, for both pages.** This issue assumes Awin (`awinmid`/`awinaffid` wrapper); `shared/affiliates.js` also accepts Booking's native `aid` (direct / CJ / Travelpayouts, the last with instant approval and no traffic minimum). Either is fine — but pick one and use it in both places. #164 tracks collapsing the duplicate Booking fields into `shared/affiliates.js` once #157 merges, after which there's only one field to fill.
- **Step 2 (Trainline) is also the planner's transport fallback.** If Omio (#164's chosen transport partner: train + coach + flight in one link) rejects us, the `camref` from this step is what the trip-block nag would use instead.
- **Steps 3 and 4 (GetYourGuide, OpenTable) are Now-page-only** — nothing in the planner touches them, so this issue remains their only home.

No change needed to the steps themselves; the sign-ups listed here are still the right ones.

{"number":314,"title":"Replace per-file cache TTLs with a published manifest","body":"Follow-up to #309, raised by the owner while reviewing the fix.

## The idea

Publish a manifest listing every downloadable data file and a hash of its contents. Fetch it on each load, and evict exactly the cached entries whose hash has moved.

## Why it's better than what we have

The current TTLs (`shared/data-cache.js`) are guesses about how fast each file changes — four days for the catalogue, one for availability, seven for descriptions. They price the same bet on every file and get it wrong in both directions at once: too long and visitors read stale data, too short and they re-download something that never changed.

A manifest gives **longer caching and fresher data at the same time**, which no TTL can. It also makes #309 structurally impossible: every file is checked against one manifest from one publish, so a visitor can't hold Thursday's catalogue beside Saturday's sidecar.

## Design notes

- **The manifest is the one file that must never carry a TTL.** Nothing can attest to its own freshness — a stale copy carries a valid hash of itself. Caching the manifest doesn't save a round-trip, it moves the staleness up one level and hides it better.
- **Marginal cost is near zero.** The planner already fetches `package.json` uncached on every load for the version pill (visible in the reporter's network trace). The manifest is the same shape of request and could absorb that one.
- **Record the hash, don't re-hash.** Store the manifest hash in the stamps map beside the entry; the freshness check is then a string compare. Re-hashing means pushing megabytes through a digest on the critical path to answer a question the bookkeeping already knows.
- **Written atomically with the assets** — same `write_derived_outputs()` call in `scraper/normalize.py`, so it can't describe a publish that didn't happen.
- **A deploy race is expected**: manifest fetched, deploy lands, asset fetched, hash disagrees. Refetch once and continue; only a mismatch surviving fresh copies of both is a real fault.
- Size is not a substitute for a hash: applying #274's correction to the Aug 7 catalogue changes 0 bytes of 3,140,534 while changing the meaning of every record.

## Relationship to the #309 fix

The join fingerprint shipped in #310 answers *"do these two published files agree with each other?"* — a generator-side question. The manifest answers *"is my cached copy the published one?"* — a client-side one, and the one that actually caused #309.

They overlap but neither subsumes the other. If this lands, the fingerprint and the 90% coverage floor become narrower backstops (a generator publishing a genuinely mismatched pair) rather than the primary defence, and the mismatch-triggered refetch path in `loadCatalogue()` could likely be retired in favour of manifest-driven eviction. Worth revisiting them together rather than leaving three overlapping mechanisms in place.

Guidance captured in `.claudinite/local/packs/static-website/RULES.md` (#310).

{"number":237,"title":"Upstream: baselining's deliver() leaves the scheduler checkout on its maintenance branch","body":"Root cause behind #231 and #141, found while correcting #235 (see #236).

The scheduler runs every due task in **one** checkout. `basics/baselining`'s `deliver()` does:

```js
git(['-C', root, 'checkout', '-B', branch]);   // .claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining/worker.mjs:447
```

and never switches back. Every task ordered after a *delivering* baselining in the same run therefore starts on a local branch with no upstream and with baselining's converge commit at HEAD. For this repo's data workers that surfaced as `preprocessing exited 128` on the bare `git push`:

- #231 — run `31016971857`, a manual `FORCE_TASKS=baselining` dispatch: `baselining: ok (agent requested)` then `refresh-tickets: preprocessing exited 128`.
- #141 — `refresh-shows`, on the daily slot baselining shares.

The blast radius is wider than a failed push: any later task that commits is committing onto baselining's branch, and any that pushes by explicit refspec would publish baselining's unreviewed converge past its own maintenance PR.

Two candidate fixes upstream, both local to `deliver()`:
- restore the previous branch after the push (record `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` first, `git checkout -` at the end, including on the failure path); or
- build and push the maintenance commit with plumbing and never touch the working tree — `pushGenerated()` in `deliver-generated.mjs` already does exactly this.

The second matches the engine's own precedent and has no restore-on-failure path to get wrong.

`.claudinite/shared/` is vendored here, so this can't be fixed in this repo — a local edit is clobbered by the next vendor refresh. #236 works around it by returning the checkout to `main` at the top of each edfringe worker.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/issues/237","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"comments":1,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-06T16:29:04Z","updated_at":"2026-08-17T03:52:36Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}
